# Klecks painting in a box

[Klecks](https://github.com/bitbof/klecks) is a layered browser painting app. Run this in a Kotlin box:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val painting = klecks(width = 800, height = 600)
```

The box opens an editable Klecks panel. Paint with its brushes, layers, and tools. Click **Submit** in
Klecks, then confirm **Submit** in its dialog to save the layered PSD and a flattened PNG in the
Field document. The status at the lower left reads **Saved in Field document** when the transfer
finishes. Running the box again restores the saved layers. A separate `channel` gives the box
another independent painting: `klecks(channel = "study", width = 400, height = 400)`.

Kotlin can read the last submitted image:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val painting = klecks()
val png: ByteArray? = painting.pngBytes()
val layeredPsd: ByteArray? = painting.psdBytes()
```

Those values update after Submit. Strokes not yet submitted are kept in the browser, so running the
box again or reopening the page brings them back until you Submit. Each PSD and PNG is limited to about 24 MB;
the panel reports a save error if either exceeds that limit. The image data is stored with the
box as document sidecars, and Field's normal document save writes it to disk.

This is a speculative integration. It uses Klecks' official embed build and its public PSD/PNG
methods. Kotlin currently reads completed paintings; live brush events and Kotlin-driven brush
editing are future work.

# Csound

[Csound](https://csound.com) is Barry Vercoe's language for sound, which grew out of the Music N
family. An *orchestra* of instruments is written as lines of opcodes, and a *score* says when each
instrument plays. Field runs Csound in-process, through its C library, in two ways:

- **as a box language**: set a box's Main Language to Csound, and its children hold `.csd` text.
  The editor highlights it and completes opcodes with their signatures. Launching a box plays it,
  and alt/option-Enter sends single instruments and score lines to the running Csound.
- **from Kotlin**: `csound(orchestra, score)` and `CsoundInstance` hold a Csound inside a Kotlin
  box, for when the Kotlin side is doing most of the work.

Either way, Csound plays through Field's audio engine, the same one Faust and Pure Data use. Data
goes both ways: control and string channels, `invalue`/`outvalue`, score events, function tables,
MIDI, and audio, as Field signals into Csound and Csound's channels back out as Field signals.

## Building libcsound

Field does not ship a Csound binary. Build one once:

```diffstatic {data-lang=bash}
./gradlew buildCsoundNative
```

This needs `cmake`, `flex`, `bison` and libsndfile (`brew install libsndfile`, or
`apt install libsndfile1-dev`), and the network the first time. It downloads the Csound 6.18.1
source, checks it against a pinned checksum, and builds the library into `build/field-csound/`.
The command-line programs, audio drivers and plugin opcodes are left out. An installed Csound
(`/Library/Frameworks/CsoundLib64.framework`, or `libcsound64.so.6.0` on Linux) works too, and
`-Dafield.csound.library=<path>` or `AFIELD_CSOUND_LIBRARY` points Field at any other one.

## A Csound box

Make a box, choose **Set Main Language: Csound** from its command palette, and connect new boxes
under it. Each child holds a `.csd`:

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=csound screenshot="assets/csound/editor.png" capture="editor" outputs="inline" requires="csound" wait="4" padding="10" timeout="180" embed=true name="csound-editor" w="900" h="620" alt="A Csound box in Field's editor. The CSD tags are blue; instr and endin are keywords; opcodes such as pluck, butterlp and outs are coloured apart (teal) from the variables asig, kcut and icps; the p-fields p4 and p5, the strings and the semicolon comments each have their own colour. In the score at the bottom, the i statements, the carry dots and the plus are highlighted."}
<CsoundSynthesizer>
<CsInstruments>
chn_k "cutoff", 1, 3, 2400, 200, 8000

instr Pluck                       ; p4 MIDI note, p5 level in dBFS
  icps  =         cpsmidinn(p4)
  asig  pluck     ampdbfs(p5), icps, icps, 0, 1
  kcut  chnget    "cutoff"
  asig  butterlp  asig, kcut
  aenv  linsegr   1, p3, 1, 0.3, 0
  outs      asig * aenv, asig * aenv
endin
</CsInstruments>
<CsScore>
i "Pluck" 0   0.5  57  -12
i .       +   .    60  .
i .       +   1.5  64  -9
</CsScore>
</CsoundSynthesizer>
```

The rate header (`sr`, `ksmps`, `nchnls`, `0dbfs`) comes from Field: the audio engine's sample rate,
`ksmps = 32`, two outputs and `0dbfs = 1`. A Csound sample of 1.0 is full scale in Field too.
Leave the header out; one in the orchestra is overridden. `<CsOptions>` is read, except for the
flags that pick a device or a file (`-o`, `-i`, `-+rtaudio`, `-M` and the like), because Field's
audio engine is the device. Text without `<CsInstruments>` is read as a bare orchestra with no score.

A `chn_k` channel starts at the default it declares: above, `chnget "cutoff"` reads 2400 until
something writes the channel. Other Csound hosts may start it at 0, which makes this `butterlp` silent there.

### The keys

| Key | Where | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **alt/option-0**, Run, Launch | anywhere | Compiles the orchestra and score into a new Csound of the box's own and plays it, replacing any earlier one. The box runs until it is stopped or the score ends. `f 0 z` in the score keeps Csound running with nothing scheduled. |
| **alt/option-Enter** | a line inside `instr … endin` | Recompiles that whole instrument into the running Csound (`csoundCompileOrc`). Notes already sounding finish with the old definition, and the next event uses the new one. |
| **alt/option-Enter** | a selection of whole instruments | Compiles the selection as it is. |
| **alt/option-Enter** | an orchestra line outside any instrument | Compiles that line (or selection) as global code, which runs once: a new `ftgen` table, a `chn_k` declaration. |
| **alt/option-Enter** | a score line or selection | Reads it into the running Csound now (`csoundReadScore`). Start times count from this moment, so `i "Pluck" 0 1 69 -9` sounds at once. |
| **alt/option-Enter** | `<CsOptions>` | Sends nothing. The box says that options apply at the next launch. |
| Stop | | Ends the performance and frees the Csound. |

alt/option-Enter needs the box to be playing, and says so if it is not. Errors from any of these, Csound's
own messages, are marked on the box line they belong to.

### Completion

Ctrl-Space offers Csound's opcodes under the heading **Csound opcodes**. Each row shows the
manual's shortest syntax line for it, named the way the manual names arguments. The panel beside
the list shows the manual's one-line description, every syntax line, the arguments with a
sentence each, the manual section and a link to the page. An opcode the manual does not describe
shows libcsound's signature instead, in Csound's type letters: `a` audio, `k` control, `i` init,
`S` string, `x` audio or control, with bracketed optional arguments and their defaults. Inside a
quoted string after `chnget`, `chnset`, `invalue` or `outvalue`, it offers the orchestra's channel
names. In the score it offers instrument numbers and names.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin capture="ui" region="window" clip-selector=".afield-suggest" screenshot="assets/csound/completion.png" transcript="assets/transcripts/csound_completion_setup.yaml" padding="6" wait="0" timeout="180" embed=true hidden=true name="csound-completion" alt="Field's completion popup in a Csound box at the prefix posc, under the header CSOUND OPCODES. The rows are poscil and poscil3, each with the manual's shortest syntax line underneath: ares poscil aamp, acps [, ifn, iphs]. The panel beside them reads High precision oscillator., then the six syntax lines of poscil in a code block, then a list of its arguments — ifn, iphs, ares, kamp, kcps — each with one sentence from the manual, and last the manual's section, Signal Generators: Basic Oscillators, and a link to csound.com/docs/manual/poscil.html."}
ui.eval("window.localStorage.removeItem('field.suggest.recency.v1'); var s=document.createElement('style');s.textContent='.tick_text{display:none !important}';document.head.appendChild(s);return 'setup';")
ui.openEditor("csound_completion")
ui.pause(900)
ui.waitForSelector(".monaco-editor", 15000.0)
ui.clickSelector(".monaco-editor")
ui.pause(300)
ui.press("Control+A")

The opcode list comes from libcsound itself, so it holds every opcode your build has compiled in.
The descriptions, syntax lines and arguments come from the Csound Reference Manual. The few opcodes
the manual does not describe, mostly deprecated ones such as `maxtab` and `mp3sr`, show their
signatures alone. The editor's highlighting reads the same list.

Hovering on an opcode in the editor shows its description and syntax, and links to its page in the
manual, for example [`butterlp`](https://csound.com/docs/manual/butterlp.html).

The descriptions are the Csound Reference Manual's: © 1986, 1992 Massachusetts Institute of
Technology (Barry L. Vercoe) and the manual's contributors, distributed under the GNU Free
Documentation License 1.2 or later. The licence and notice ship beside the vocabulary as
`csound-manual-COPYING.txt`.

### Line notes

Rest the cursor on a line to see its note:

- on a score `i` line, which instrument it plays and where that is defined, or that this orchestra
  has no such instrument;
- on a line that declares or uses a channel (`chn_k`, `chnget`, `chnset`, `invalue`, `outvalue`),
  the channel's value in the playing Csound, read live.

## Talking to a playing Csound box from Kotlin

`csoundOf("name")` finds the playing Csound box of that name in the document. Its `csound` is the
running `CsoundInstance`, and its `node` is that Csound's place in Field's audio graph:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val pluck = csoundOf("pluck").csound

pluck.setChannel("cutoff", 900)                 // chnget "cutoff" sees it on the next k-cycle
pluck.setStringChannel("voice", "from Kotlin")  // an S channel
println(pluck.channel("level"))                 // what chnset last wrote

[57, 60, 64, 69].forEachIndexed { k, note ->
    pluck.event("i \"Pluck\" ${k * 0.5} 0.5 $note -12")   // p-fields from Kotlin values
}

pluck.onOutvalue("level") { v -> println("Reverb rms $v") }   // outvalue "level", krms
pluck.setInvalue("gain", 0.5)                                  // invalue "gain"
pluck.noteOn(0, 64, 90)                                        // MIDI, to massign'ed instruments
```

What each of these does, and on which thread:

- **Control and string channels.** `setChannel`, `channel`, `setStringChannel` and `stringChannel`
  read and write Csound's channel bus directly. Csound locks the bus itself, so they are safe from
  any thread. `hints("cutoff")` returns the default and range a `chn_k` declared, which is where
  `csoundControls` gets its slider ranges.
- **`outvalue` and `invalue`.** Csound calls Field on its rendering thread, the audio thread when
  live. Field stores the value there and runs your callback on the main thread, never on the audio
  thread. A k-rate `outvalue` runs every control cycle, 1500 times a second, so its callback runs
  once per frame, and only when the value changed. A string `outvalue` is delivered each time it
  changes. `invalue` reads numbers only: Csound does not tell the host how large an `invalue`
  string buffer is, so send strings with `setStringChannel` and read them with `chnget`.
- **Score events.** `event` queues a score line, delivered at the start of the next audio block.
- **MIDI.** `noteOn`, `noteOff`, `controlChange` and `midi(status, d1, d2)` queue bytes that
  Csound's host-MIDI input reads on the next block. `massign`, `notnum`, `veloc` and `midic7`
  work as they do with a device.
- **Tables.** `table(n)` reads function table `n`. `writeTable(n, values)` overwrites it
  (`csoundTableCopyIn`), and the next block plays the new contents. `tableLength(n)` is its size.

## Audio in both directions

Field signals go into Csound through a-rate channels, and Csound's channels and outputs come back
out as Field signals:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val fx = csoundOf("fx")
fx.node.connect("in", SawOsc(Param(110f)) * Param(0.15f))   // ain chnget "in"
fx.node.audioOut("wet").pan(-0.5f)                           // chnset aL, "wet"
```

`node.outL` and `node.outR` are Csound's `outs` as two Field signals. All of these are rendered on
the audio thread as part of the Csound node's own block, so they stay sample-aligned with the rest
of Field's graph. Two things to know about timing:

- Csound performs whole `ksmps` blocks, 32 frames here. Audio into Csound, through `connect` or
  `ins`, is delayed by exactly one block, 32 frames or 0.67 ms at 48 kHz, so that every block has a
  whole control period of input whatever size the engine's buffer is.
- Audio out of Csound is not delayed further. It is in step with the block Field asked for.

The same holds offline. `renderSignalsOffline` advances any number of signals through the same audio
blocks, without a device, which is how this box measures a Csound filter on a Field sine:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val cs = afield.audio.csound.CsoundInstance("""
instr Filter
  ain   chnget    "in"
  alow  butterlp  ain, 500
        chnset    alow, "low"
endin
""", "i \"Filter\" 0 z")
val node = cs.node(audioIn = mapOf("in" to SineOsc(Param(1000f))))
val (dry, low) = renderSignalsOffline(0.5, SineOsc(Param(1000f)), node.audioOut("low"))
cs.close()
```

It prints a gain of 0.2420. A second-order Butterworth lowpass passes twice its cutoff at
1/√(1 + 2⁴) = 0.2425.

## Csound inside a Kotlin box

When the Kotlin is the larger part, `csound` compiles an orchestra and score inside a Kotlin box and
returns a `CsoundLaunch`. Return it as the box's last expression to hear it:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val drone = csound("""
chn_k "pitch", 1, 2, 110, 55, 440
chn_k "cutoff", 1, 2, 1200, 200, 6000
instr 1
  kf chnget "pitch"
  kc chnget "cutoff"
  kf port kf, 0.05
  kc port kc, 0.05
  a1 vco2 0.12, kf
  a1 moogladder a1, kc, 0.3
  outs a1, a1
endin
""", "i1 0 z")
csoundControls(drone)
drone
```

`csoundControls` makes one slider per input `chn_k` channel, using the range Csound itself recorded
for it. `csound(..., audioIn = mapOf("in" to signal))` feeds Field signals in. `launch.audioOut`,
`outL` and `outR` take Csound's audio back out, and `every(seconds) { event(...) }` writes a score
from Kotlin on the main loop. `csoundOffline(orchestra, score)` renders with no audio device and
shows a player and a waveform.

## The demo

Open csound_demo from the welcome screen's starting points. It is a Csound root with three Csound
boxes (**pluck**, **fx**, **typo**) and five Kotlin boxes that use each of the directions above.

See also: [Faust](faust.md) and [Pure Data](pure_data.md), the other languages that play through
the same audio engine, and [How to make sound in Field](sound.md).

## Talking to a playing Csound box from Kotlin

`csoundOf("name")` finds the playing Csound box of that name in the document. Its `csound` is the
running `CsoundInstance`, and its `node` is that Csound's place in Field's audio graph:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val pluck = csoundOf("pluck").csound

pluck.setChannel("cutoff", 900)                 // chnget "cutoff" sees it on the next k-cycle
pluck.setStringChannel("voice", "from Kotlin")  // an S channel
println(pluck.channel("level"))                 // what chnset last wrote

[57, 60, 64, 69].forEachIndexed { k, note ->
    pluck.event("i \"Pluck\" ${k * 0.5} 0.5 $note -12")   // p-fields from Kotlin values
}

pluck.onOutvalue("level") { v -> println("Reverb rms $v") }   // outvalue "level", krms
pluck.setInvalue("gain", 0.5)                                  // invalue "gain"
pluck.noteOn(0, 64, 90)                                        // MIDI, to massign'ed instruments
```

What each of these does, and on which thread:

- **Control and string channels.** `setChannel`, `channel`, `setStringChannel` and `stringChannel`
  read and write Csound's channel bus directly. Csound locks the bus itself, so they are safe from
  any thread. `hints("cutoff")` returns the default and range a `chn_k` declared, which is where
  `csoundControls` gets its slider ranges.
- **`outvalue` and `invalue`.** Csound calls Field on its rendering thread, the audio thread when
  live. Field stores the value there and runs your callback on the main thread, never on the audio
  thread. A k-rate `outvalue` runs every control cycle, 1500 times a second, so its callback runs
  once per frame, and only when the value changed. A string `outvalue` is delivered each time it
  changes. `invalue` reads numbers only: Csound does not tell the host how large an `invalue`
  string buffer is, so send strings with `setStringChannel` and read them with `chnget`.
- **Score events.** `event` queues a score line, delivered at the start of the next audio block.
- **MIDI.** `noteOn`, `noteOff`, `controlChange` and `midi(status, d1, d2)` queue bytes that
  Csound's host-MIDI input reads on the next block. `massign`, `notnum`, `veloc` and `midic7`
  work as they do with a device.
- **Tables.** `table(n)` reads function table `n`. `writeTable(n, values)` overwrites it
  (`csoundTableCopyIn`), and the next block plays the new contents. `tableLength(n)` is its size.

## Audio in both directions

Field signals go into Csound through a-rate channels, and Csound's channels and outputs come back
out as Field signals:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val fx = csoundOf("fx")
fx.node.connect("in", SawOsc(Param(110f)) * Param(0.15f))   // ain chnget "in"
fx.node.audioOut("wet").pan(-0.5f)                           // chnset aL, "wet"
```

`node.outL` and `node.outR` are Csound's `outs` as two Field signals. All of these are rendered on
the audio thread as part of the Csound node's own block, so they stay sample-aligned with the rest
of Field's graph. Two things to know about timing:

- Csound performs whole `ksmps` blocks, 32 frames here. Audio into Csound, through `connect` or
  `ins`, is delayed by exactly one block, 32 frames or 0.67 ms at 48 kHz, so that every block has a
  whole control period of input whatever size the engine's buffer is.
- Audio out of Csound is not delayed further. It is in step with the block Field asked for.

The same holds offline. `renderSignalsOffline` advances any number of signals through the same audio
blocks, without a device, which is how this box measures a Csound filter on a Field sine:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val cs = afield.audio.csound.CsoundInstance("""
instr Filter
  ain   chnget    "in"
  alow  butterlp  ain, 500
        chnset    alow, "low"
endin
""", "i \"Filter\" 0 z")
val node = cs.node(audioIn = mapOf("in" to SineOsc(Param(1000f))))
val (dry, low) = renderSignalsOffline(0.5, SineOsc(Param(1000f)), node.audioOut("low"))
cs.close()
```

This excerpt returns the dry and lowpass sample arrays. The full `csound_demo` starting point
measures their RMS ratio and prints a gain of 0.2420. A second-order Butterworth lowpass
passes a signal at twice its cutoff with gain 1/√(1 + 2⁴) = 0.2425.

## Csound inside a Kotlin box

When the Kotlin is the larger part, `csound` compiles an orchestra and score inside a Kotlin box and
returns a `CsoundLaunch`. Return it as the box's last expression to hear it:

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val drone = csound("""
chn_k "pitch", 1, 2, 110, 55, 440
chn_k "cutoff", 1, 2, 1200, 200, 6000
instr 1
  kf chnget "pitch"
  kc chnget "cutoff"
  kf port kf, 0.05
  kc port kc, 0.05
  a1 vco2 0.12, kf
  a1 moogladder a1, kc, 0.3
  outs a1, a1
endin
""", "i1 0 z")
csoundControls(drone)
drone
```

`csoundControls` makes one slider per input `chn_k` channel, using the range Csound itself recorded
for it. `csound(..., audioIn = mapOf("in" to signal))` feeds Field signals in. `launch.audioOut`,
`outL` and `outR` take Csound's audio back out, and `every(seconds) { event(...) }` writes a score
from Kotlin on the main loop. `csoundOffline(orchestra, score)` renders with no audio device and
shows a player and a waveform.

## The demo

Open csound_demo from the welcome screen's starting points. It is a Csound root with three Csound
boxes (**pluck**, **fx**, **typo**) and five Kotlin boxes that use each of the directions above.

See also: [Faust](faust.md) and [Pure Data](pure_data.md), the other languages that play through
the same audio engine, and [How to make sound in Field](sound.md).

before: # Interactive Guides A guide is a box that walks someone through a document they have not seen before. You write it in the box, and the person following it gets notes, moving selections and callout lines over the live document itself. A guide can: - show a note next to a box, - move the editor to a property and line, - branch through callbacks, - render live values into Markdown templates, - attach a discussion thread, - draw callout lines to boxes or exact code lines. A guide is a `slideShow { ... }` block. Each `step("...")` is one stage of the guide, and `markdownNote(...)` in a step writes the note the reader sees. A guide's notes and callout lines come and go with its steps. For marks that stay on the canvas, such as a hand-drawn diagram beside the boxes it explains or arrows a box draws for itself, see [Drawing and Notation](drawing_and_notation.md), the Excalidraw layer (`alt/option-d`) that is saved with the document. ## A three-step guide This box is a whole guide: three steps, each with a note and a link to the next one. Run it and its first note opens beside the box. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/interactive_guides/three_step_tour.png" wait="8" capture="box" outputs="none" embed=true name="three-step-tour" w="560" h="140" padding="28" alt="The guide box on the left with a green running dot, and beside it the first note: the heading A three-step tour, the sentence saying the note belongs to the box on the left and to follow the link at the bottom, and a Next link."} :::static val guide = thisBox val show = slideShow { step("Hello") { markdownNote( """ ## A three-step tour This note belongs to the box on the left. Follow the link at the bottom to move on. [[next]] """.trimIndent(), animated = true ) selectBox(guide) } step("The code") { markdownNote( """ ## Each step is a `step(...)` The editor now shows this box's code. [[back]] [[next]] """.trimIndent() ) selectBox(guide, property = "code", line = 5, highlight = 5) } step("Done") { markdownNote( """ ## That is the whole tour [[home:Start again]] [[finish]] """.trimIndent() ) } } runBlocking { show.start() } ``` `slideShow { ... }` builds the guide and stores it on the box; nothing is shown until `show.start()` opens the first step. `animated = true` types the first note in rather than showing it all at once. `selectBox(box)` selects a box, and with `property`, `line` and `highlight` it also opens the editor on that property, scrolls to a line and marks it. Use `selectBoxByName("name")` for a box you do not have in a variable; it searches the whole document. ## Moving between steps The reader moves through a guide with links in its notes. A `[[...]]` shortcut in a Markdown note becomes one of them: | shortcut | goes to | label | | --- | --- | --- | | `[[next]]`, `[[start]]` | the next step | Next →, Start → | | `[[back]]`, `[[previous]]`, `[[prev]]` | the previous step | ← Back | | `[[home]]` | the first step | Home | | `[[stop]]`, `[[finish]]` | closes the guide | Finish | Give a link your own label after a colon: `[[next:Onward →]]`, `[[home:Start again]]`. The shortcuts are ordinary links to `#slideshow:next`, `#slideshow:previous`, `#slideshow:home` and `#slideshow:stop`, so a note written in HTML with `note(...)` can use those directly, and `#slideshow:2` jumps to a step by number, counting from 0. From code the same moves are `show.next()`, `show.previous()`, `show.home()`, `show.stop()` and `show.goToStep(n)`, all called from a coroutine. `show.hasNext()` and `show.hasPrevious()` say whether there is anywhere to go. This guide opens on its second step, whose note uses each kind of link, and marks line 13, the line that writes those links: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/interactive_guides/navigation.png" wait="5" capture="window-editor" outputs="none" embed=true name="guide-navigation" w="240" h="60" padding="12" alt="The Field window. On the left the small guide box, selected, and beside it the second step's note, headed Moving between steps, ending in four links: Back, First step, Onward and Finish. On the right the editor shows the guide's code with a red mark in the gutter at line 13, the line holding the four bracket shortcuts."} :::static val guide = thisBox val show = slideShow { step("Start") { markdownNote("## Step one\n[[next]]") } step("Links") { markdownNote( """ ## Moving between steps Step two of three. Each link below came from a `[[...]]` shortcut. [[back]] [[home:First step]] [[next:Onward →]] [[stop]] """.trimIndent() ) selectBox(guide, property = "code", line = 13, highlight = 13) } step("End") { markdownNote("## The last step\n[[back]] [[finish]]") } } runBlocking { show.goToStep(1) } ``` A document can hold several guides. The links in a note always drive the guide that opened it. ## Doing something as a step opens or closes `onEnter { ... }` runs each time the reader arrives at a step, before its note is shown, and `onExit { ... }` runs as they leave it, including when the guide is stopped. Use them to launch the box a step is about and stop it again, or to update a value the note shows. Both blocks may suspend. The [slideshow_guide](agent_transcripts.md#slideshow_guide) starting point counts visits to one of its steps this way, and shows the count in that step's note with a `{{visits}}` template, described next. ## Add callbacks and live template values An interactive step uses a `#custom:name` link in the note body, a `linkCallback("name") { ... }` handler in the step to receive it, and `{{propertyName}}` template expansion for the live values. Above them the line reads Version: 1.0.0, and the footer reads Count: 3 and Choice: Balanced Mode."} :::static var clickCount = 3 var userChoice = "Balanced Mode" val version = "1.0.0" val host = thisBox println("interactive guide ready") val show = slideShow { step("Interactive Choices") { markdownNote( """ ## Interactive Guides with Callbacks Version: **{{version}}** - [Increment](#custom:incrementCounter) - [Choose performance mode](#custom:choiceA) - [Choose quality mode](#custom:choiceB) Count: **{{clickCount}}** Choice: **{{userChoice}}** """.trimIndent() ) linkCallback("incrementCounter") { clickCount += 1 here.properties["clickCount"] = clickCount show.goToStep(show.currentStepIndex) } linkCallback("choiceA") { userChoice = "Performance Mode" here.properties["userChoice"] = userChoice show.goToStep(show.currentStepIndex) notify("Selected: Performance Mode", "slideshow") } linkCallback("choiceB") { userChoice = "Quality Mode" here.properties["userChoice"] = userChoice show.goToStep(show.currentStepIndex) notify("Selected: Quality Mode", "slideshow") } selectBox(host, property = "code") } } runBlocking { show.start() } ``` A template value can come from `this.properties[...]`, from a Kotlin variable the box has already run, or from the shared template helpers the slideshow runtime exposes. When a callback changes state, call `show.goToStep(show.currentStepIndex)` to rerender the current step immediately. That updates `{{clickCount}}` and `{{userChoice}}` without leaving the slide. A value that comes from a box property or a script variable is inserted as text: `<`, `>`, `&` and quotes are escaped, so a property holding `hi` shows those characters rather than bold text. Put markup in the note itself, not in the value. ## Annotations and code callouts Annotations let a note point at an exact target. - `annotate(...)` points from the note to a box. - `annotateToLine(...)` points to an exact property and line inside the editor. Use them when a sentence is about one box, one property, or one line. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/interactive_guides/annotations.png" wait="5" capture="window-editor" outputs="none" embed=true name="guide-annotations" w="240" h="60" padding="12" alt="The Field window. On the left the small guide box, selected, with a green arrowhead at its top-right corner, and beside it the note headed Annotation Lines with its two bullets. An orange dashed line runs from the note across the canvas and curves down to the editor's left edge, ending at the top of line 17. On the right the editor shows the snippet, with a red mark in the gutter at line 17, the selectBox call."} :::static val host = thisBox host.name = "guide-annotations" val show = slideShow { step("Annotations") { markdownNote( """ ## Annotation Lines Guides can point at whole boxes and exact code lines. - the green line targets the box, - the orange dashed line targets line 17 in this guide box. """.trimIndent(), animated = true ) selectBox(host, property = "code", line = 17, highlight = 17) annotate( id = "target-box", targetBox = host, color = "rgba(128, 255, 164, 0.8)", strokeWidth = 2.5 ) annotateToLine( id = "target-line", targetBox = host, property = "code", line = 17, color = "rgba(255, 180, 100, 0.8)", strokeWidth = 2.0, dashed = true ) } } runBlocking { show.start() } ``` For line-level teaching, combine `selectBox(...)`, `line = ...`, `highlight = ...`, and `annotateToLine(...)`. Use `withChat(id = "templateId")` when multiple template instances should share one thread. [[back]] [[next]] """.trimIndent() ) withChat(id = "templateId") selectBox(host, property = "code") } } runBlocking { show.start() } ``` Use per-slide chat when comments should stay attached to a specific step instead of floating beside the whole guide. The capture above shows the collapsed Discussion UI. The Python chat-service prototype has been retired; `withChat()` and its UI remain available for a later redesign. Without a compatible external backend, message loads and posts fail, while the rest of the slideshow still renders. ### Setting up the chat server Field no longer bundles a chat server. Its retained JVM proxy uses `CHAT_SERVER_URL`, defaulting to `http://localhost:5002`, if a compatible service is provided separately. A browser identity can still be selected with `?file=myguide&username=student1`; the default is `anonymous`. The retained bridge is described in [`dev_docs/GUIDE_CHAT_QUICKSTART.md`](https://github.com/OpenEndedGroup/Field4/blob/main/dev_docs/GUIDE_CHAT_QUICKSTART.md). ## Notes outside a guide The note overlay works without a guide too. `showMarkdownNote(...)` (or `showNote(...)` for HTML) opens a note beside the box that calls it, with the same `{{...}}` templates, and `hideNote()` closes it. You write it in the box, and the person following it gets notes, moving selections and callout lines over the live document itself. A guide can: - show a note next to a box, - move the editor to a property and line, - branch through callbacks, - render live values into Markdown templates, - attach a discussion thread, - draw callout lines to boxes or exact code lines. A guide is a `slideShow { ... }` block. Each `step("...")` is one stage of the guide, and `markdownNote(...)` in a step writes the note the reader sees. A guide's notes and callout lines come and go with its steps. For marks that stay on the canvas, such as a hand-drawn diagram beside the boxes it explains or arrows a box draws for itself, see [Drawing and Notation](drawing_and_notation.md), the Excalidraw layer (`alt/option-d`) that is saved with the document. ## A three-step guide This box is a whole guide: three steps, each with a note and a link to the next one. Run it and its first note opens beside the box. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/interactive_guides/three_step_tour.png" wait="8" capture="box" outputs="none" embed=true name="three-step-tour" w="560" h="140" padding="28" alt="The guide box on the left with a green running dot, and beside it the first note: the heading A three-step tour, the sentence saying the note belongs to the box on the left and to follow the link at the bottom, and a Next link."} :::static val guide = thisBox val show = slideShow { step("Hello") { markdownNote( """ ## A three-step tour This note belongs to the box on the left. Follow the link at the bottom to move on. [[next]] """.trimIndent(), animated = true ) selectBox(guide) } step("The code") { markdownNote( """ ## Each step is a `step(...)` The editor now shows this box's code. [[back]] [[next]] """.trimIndent() ) selectBox(guide, property = "code", line = 5, highlight = 5) } step("Done") { markdownNote( """ ## That is the whole tour [[home:Start again]] [[finish]] """.trimIndent() ) } } runBlocking { show.start() } ``` `slideShow { ... }` builds the guide and stores it on the box; nothing is shown until `show.start()` opens the first step. `animated = true` types the first note in rather than showing it all at once. `selectBox(box)` selects a box, and with `property`, `line` and `highlight` it also opens the editor on that property, scrolls to a line and marks it. Use `selectBoxByName("name")` for a box you do not have in a variable; it searches the whole document. ## Moving between steps The reader moves through a guide with links in its notes. A `[[...]]` shortcut in a Markdown note becomes one of them: | shortcut | goes to | label | | --- | --- | --- | | `[[next]]`, `[[start]]` | the next step | Next →, Start → | | `[[back]]`, `[[previous]]`, `[[prev]]` | the previous step | ← Back | | `[[home]]` | the first step | Home | | `[[stop]]`, `[[finish]]` | closes the guide | Finish | Give a link your own label after a colon: `[[next:Onward →]]`, `[[home:Start again]]`. The shortcuts are ordinary links to `#slideshow:next`, `#slideshow:previous`, `#slideshow:home` and `#slideshow:stop`, so a note written in HTML with `note(...)` can use those directly, and `#slideshow:2` jumps to a step by number, counting from 0. When a callback changes state, call `show.goToStep(show.currentStepIndex)` to rerender the current step immediately. That updates `{{clickCount}}` and `{{userChoice}}` without leaving the slide. # Spatial artificial life

*Every public declaration used below is listed, with its KDoc, in the codebase reference:
[`alife.kt`](reference/alife.md#alife-kt), [`alife_ca.kt`](reference/alife.md#alife-ca-kt),
[`alife_continuous.kt`](reference/alife.md#alife-continuous-kt),
[`alife_agents.kt`](reference/alife.md#alife-agents-kt),
[`alife_lsystem.kt`](reference/alife.md#alife-lsystem-kt) and
[`alife_field.kt`](reference/alife.md#alife-field-kt). Start from
[what's already in the box](reference/index.md).*

Artificial life is the study of systems whose interesting behaviour is not in their rules. You write
down something local and small (count your neighbours, follow the strongest smell, grow toward the
nearest unclaimed space) and something global and large happens that the rule never mentions: a
spaceship, a coastline, a transport network, a dendrite with a fractional dimension. This page is
about the *spatial* half of that: grids, continuous fields and populations of agents. The
graph-rewriting half lives in [`growing.kt`](reference/data.md#growing-kt) and
[interaction nets](interaction_nets_examples.md), the constraint-based generative half is
[Wave Function Collapse](wfc_examples.md), and the half where a *moving* point cloud carries a
decaying graph with it is [graphs that change while you
watch](dynamic_graph_systems_examples.md).

Almost any local rule applied to noise looks organic, so each example here prints a measurement
beside a *control*: the same setup with one ingredient removed, which gets the number wrong. A
glider's every live cell is displaced by exactly `(1, 1)` after four generations, and the same seed
under a rule one birth-count away is displaced by nothing at all. A flock of 400 agents reaches a
polarization of 0.69 where 400 independent headings would give 0.044, and the same initial state
with the alignment term zeroed reaches 0.073.

??? aside "Where the numbers come from"
    `afield.examples.stdlib.AlifeGallery` renders the figures below in CI and asserts, for each, the
    statistic its control fails, so the numbers printed here are the numbers it asserts.

## Source files

Six dependency-free files built on the existing [imaging](imaging_examples.md) and
[mesh](mesh_examples.md) families. Nothing here reimplements convolution, connected-component
labelling, colour mapping or marching cubes:

- **`alife.kt`** — [`IntGrid`](reference/alife.md#alife-kt-intgrid), the toroidal-or-bounded integer
  lattice; the grid↔[`Img`](imaging_examples.md) bridges; and, mostly, the measurement layer that
  the rest of the family makes its claims through —
  [`polarization`](reference/alife.md#alife-kt) and its random baseline,
  [`blobShapes`](reference/alife.md#alife-kt) (the isoperimetric ratio that tells spots from
  stripes), [`correlationLength`](reference/alife.md#alife-kt),
  [`topShare`](reference/alife.md#alife-kt) and
  [`massRadiusDimension`](reference/alife.md#alife-kt).
- **`alife_ca.kt`** — [`LifeRule`](reference/alife.md#alife-ca-kt-liferule) parsed from `B3/S23`,
  named Life patterns, exact cycle detection, cyclic multi-state CA, Wolfram's elementary 1-D rules as
  a space-time raster, and a 3-D life-like CA on [`IntVolume`](reference/alife.md#alife-ca-kt-intvolume).
- **`alife_continuous.kt`** — mass-conserving diffusion, Gray–Scott reaction–diffusion,
  Gierer–Meinhardt Turing patterns, and Lenia.
- **`alife_agents.kt`** — boids, a Physarum deposit–sense–move population, and diffusion-limited
  aggregation with two control models.
- **`alife_lsystem.kt`** — a bracketed, parametric, optionally stochastic L-system with a turtle that
  emits [`FLine`](fline_examples.md)s, and space-colonization branching.
- **`alife_field.kt`** — the [inline `ToHTML` views](#evaluating-one-of-these-in-a-box-the-inline-views),
  kept in their own file so the five above name nothing from Field's visualizer.

Two later files extend the agent side along an axis this page does not walk through. Every system
above advances a whole population with one call and one parameter block, so two agents differ only
in their state and never in what they are trying to do:

- **`alife_script.kt`** — [`ScriptWorld`](reference/alife.md#alife-script-kt-scriptworld) gives each
  agent its own suspending *program* on a fixed-step clock: `forever`, `phase(name)`, `parallel`,
  `moveUntil`, and steering composed from whichever behaviours are active right now. The same seed
  gives the same run, bit for bit, across processes.
- **`alife_walls.kt`** — and an environment for it to run in:
  [`ScriptObstacle`](reference/alife.md#alife-walls-kt-scriptobstacle), swept circle collision with
  a per-agent [`WallResponse`](reference/alife.md#alife-walls-kt-wallresponse), `avoidWalls` and
  `cling`, and a radius-aware [`NavGrid`](reference/alife.md#alife-walls-kt-navgrid) so `route()`
  can go round a barrier that direct `seek` presses into. On an S-maze, over 96 agents, routed
  `seek` arrives 0.990 of the time against 0.000 for direct `seek` at the same budget.

Both are worked through in [section 12](#12-agents-that-run-programs-and-a-world-to-run-them-in),
which also says where to find them as documents you can open and edit.

Limits:

- **CPU only.** These are reference implementations you can read. The GPU story is
  [Field 4](reference/graphics.md), [StackSL](stacksl_examples.md) and
  [RectSL](rectsl_examples.md). Four systems from this family's neighbourhood do run on the GPU, as
  shaders you can edit: [diffusion-limited aggregation](afield_four_graphics.md#diffusion-limited-aggregation),
  [Biham–Middleton–Levine traffic](afield_four_graphics.md#bml-traffic), a
  [lattice Boltzmann fluid](afield_four_graphics.md#lattice-boltzmann) and a
  [forest fire](afield_four_graphics.md#forest-fire).
- **No named Lenia lifeform.** Reproducing Orbium needs its exact published initial array, which this
  family does not ship. What it does instead is [prove the discrete limit](#5-lenia) and report a
  measured phase trichotomy.
- **`O(N²)` neighbour search in the agent models.** A spatial hash is right for 50 000 agents and is a
  different piece of code; these flocks are a few hundred agents and legibility wins.
- **Explicit Euler integration** for the continuous systems, with the stability bound stated as a
  `require` rather than silently clamped.

## 1. Conway's Life

`B3/S23` is the most-studied dynamical system in computing, which is exactly why it is the right place
to start: there are *facts* about it to be checked. The glider translates one cell diagonally every
four generations. The block is a still life. The blinker has period two. And the R-pentomino (five
cells) runs for 1103 generations, peaks at a population of 319 at generation 821, and settles to 116
cells, six of which are gliders still flying away.

Those R-pentomino figures are about an *unbounded* board. On a board with walls the
gliders are destroyed, and the system instead becomes exactly periodic at generation 1164 with 110
cells. Both answers are correct; they are answers to different questions. So the box below runs on a
620-wide board (wide enough that no glider can reach an edge in 1103 generations) and asserts
[`liveBounds`](reference/alife.md#alife-kt-intgrid) to *confirm* the walls never took part rather than
assuming it.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/alife_examples/life.png" wait="12.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}

// Conway's Life. Every claim here is about an object that predates this code, stated as an
// integer-grid equality rather than as an observation about a picture.
val glider = LifePatterns.glider.centeredOn(40, 40)
println("glider, 4 generations: rigid translation = " + translationBetween(glider, glider.stepTimes(LIFE, 4)))
println("glider, 8 generations: rigid translation = " + translationBetween(glider, glider.stepTimes(LIFE, 8)))

// The control: one birth count away and the same seed is not a spaceship at all.
println("same seed under B34/S23, 4 generations: " +
    translationBetween(glider, glider.stepTimes(lifeRule("B34/S23"), 4)))

val block = LifePatterns.block.centeredOn(20, 20)
println("block is bit-identical after one step: " + block.step(LIFE).sameCellsAs(block))
println("blinker's detected period: " + LifePatterns.blinker.centeredOn(20, 20).runUntilCycle(LIFE, 20).period)
println("toad's detected period: " + LifePatterns.toad.centeredOn(20, 20).runUntilCycle(LIFE, 20).period)

// The R-pentomino. The textbook figures -- peak 319 at generation 821, then 116 cells from
// generation 1103 -- are facts about an UNBOUNDED board: six of those 116 cells are gliders still
// in flight. So it needs room. 620 wide gives every glider more than the 1103/4 cells it can
// travel, and liveBounds() confirms nothing reached an edge rather than assuming it.
var g = LifePatterns.rPentomino.centeredOn(620, 620, wrap = false)
var peak = 0
var peakAt = 0
for (gen in 1..1103) {
    g = g.step(LIFE)
    val pop = g.population()
    if (pop > peak) { peak = pop; peakAt = gen }
}
val b = g.liveBounds()!!
println("R-pentomino peak population " + peak + " at generation " + peakAt)
println("population at generation 1103 = " + g.population() +
    ", live cells " + b[0] + " clear of the board edge")

:::fold draw the glider's first five generations, twelve pixels to a cell
showImg(
    montage(
        (0..4).map { "gen " + it to LifePatterns.glider.centeredOn(16, 16).stepTimes(LIFE, it).toImg(2).upscaleNearest(12) },
        columns = 5, cellSide = 200
    ),
    caption = "one glider, five generations: the same shape displaced by (1, 1)"
)
:::endfold
```

![five 16-cell boards in a row, one glider on each: the same five-cell shape at generations 0 to 4, each one cell further down and to the right than the last](assets/alife_examples/life.png)

[`translationBetween`](reference/alife.md#alife-kt) is not a centroid comparison. It aligns the two
patterns' bounding boxes, shifts one by that offset, and then demands **exact cell-by-cell equality**, so
a pattern that moved *and* changed shape returns `null`. A wrong rule cannot fluke that: the
`B34/S23` line above prints `null`.

### The two objects, moving

Two panels, 400 generations, two generations per displayed frame: slow enough that the glider's
four-generation cycle is legible rather than a strobe.

Left: the glider, on a **16-cell torus**, twenty-four pixels to a cell. It laps that board every 64
generations and does it six times over, so if you watch one edge you see it leave and re-enter from the
other. That is the same claim the montage above makes, and the same claim `translationBetween` asserts, in
the form where it is obvious.

Right: the R-pentomino on a **64-cell walled** board, with its live population in the caption. This is
the walled question, not the unbounded one the numbers above are about: those need 620 cells, and 620
cells at one pixel each is a video whose interesting part is four pixels wide. Same rule, same seed,
different board, and what it shows is the shape of the thing: five cells, a violent expansion, then a
long quieting-down toward something stationary.

??? aside "Why the boards are so small"
    A glider is five live cells, so the board size decides what fraction of the frame ever changes. On a
    48-cell torus that is **0.2 %** of the pixels: the motion is perfect and the picture is almost still.
    Sixteen cells makes the same five cells **2 %** of the panel, which takes the mean absolute luma
    difference between the clip's first and last frames from **1.47** of 255 to **5.26**, with half the
    change arriving by 37 % of its length. A frame wants to be the size of the thing being claimed.

## 2. Wolfram's elementary rules

A one-dimensional automaton's behaviour is two-dimensional, so
[`elementaryCa`](reference/alife.md#alife-ca-kt) returns the whole **space-time diagram** as an
`IntGrid`: one row per generation, time downward. Every famous statement about these 256 rules is a
statement about this picture.

Rule 90 is `left XOR right`, and from a single seed its space-time diagram **is Pascal's triangle mod
2**, the Sierpiński gasket.
[`sierpinskiReference`](reference/alife.md#alife-ca-kt) computes that from Kummer's theorem
(`C(n, k)` is odd exactly when `n and k == k`) without running a cellular automaton at all. So the
equality between them is a cross-check between two unrelated computations, not a stepper agreeing with
itself, and it holds in all 32 896 cells. A second, independent oracle comes free: row `g` of that
diagram holds exactly `2^popcount(g)` live cells (Gould's sequence).

Rule 184 is the traffic rule, and it conserves the number of live cells **exactly**, forever. Rule 90
does not, which is the control that stops "184 conserves density" from being a property of the harness.

## 3. Cyclic cellular automata

A cyclic cellular automaton has `k` states arranged in a ring. A cell in state `s` advances to `s + 1`
as soon as at least `threshold` of its neighbours are *already* in `s + 1`; otherwise it waits. Nothing
can skip a state, and there is no way back, so the only durable structures are rotating bands.

The measurement that makes "it self-organised" checkable is
[`cyclicAdvanceFraction`](reference/alife.md#alife-ca-kt). In an **uncorrelated** soup a cell can advance
exactly when one of its eight Moore neighbours happens to hold its successor state, which is
`1 - (1 - 1/k)^8`: a closed form, not a threshold. For `k = 14` that is 0.4473, and the measurement is
0.4483. Four hundred generations later every cell is being driven by a neighbour and the fraction pins
at **1.0000**, which is something no uncorrelated field does at any `k`.

The second pair of panels is the excitable corner of the parameter space (six states, threshold three,
radius two), which curls into visible spiral cores. That is a different *phase*, and the difference is
reported as a length scale rather than left to the eye, though note the direction: the wider
neighbourhood gives the **smaller** correlation length, because the spiral arms are narrow.

??? note "This statistic's floor is 0.632, not 0"
    [`correlationLength`](reference/alife.md#alife-kt) is the lag at which the direction-averaged
    autocorrelation first falls to `1/e`, linearly interpolated. For a field with *no* correlation at all
    the interpolation runs from `ac(0) = 1` straight to `ac(1) ≈ 0`, so the answer is `1 − 1/e = 0.632`:
    a floor, reached from below by nothing. So compare a settled field against its own pixels
    *shuffled*, which lands on that floor to six decimal places, rather than against a chosen
    constant. A checkerboard, the shortest wavelength a lattice holds, reads exactly
    `(1 − 1/e)/(4/3) = 0.4741`, which is as low as this statistic can go.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/alife_examples/cyclic.png" wait="6.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}

## 4. Gray–Scott reaction–diffusion

Two coupled fields, `u` (substrate) and `v` (autocatalyst), the reaction `U + 2V → 3V` with `V → P`,
and two numbers: a feed rate `F` and a kill rate `k`. The entire zoo of morphologies is a function of
those two numbers. Two knobs producing that much variety is why Gray–Scott is the canonical
morphogenesis model.

Spots and a labyrinth can have *identical* coverage, identical mean and identical variance. Nothing in a
histogram separates them. What does separate them is the **shape** of their features, and
[`morphology()`](reference/alife.md#alife-continuous-kt-morphologyreport) measures it: the
isoperimetric ratio `P²/4πA` (1 for a disc, growing without bound as a region gets thinner and more
convoluted) and the share of the covered area held by the single largest connected feature.

The numbers below, from the run in the box: the spots preset gives 329 separate features with a median
ratio of **0.80** and a largest-blob share of **0.008**; the two labyrinth presets give 24 and 34
features with ratios of **2.5** and **2.4** and largest shares of **0.64** and **0.45**. Three times
less round, and dominated by one connected structure. The `holes` preset is the inverse morphology and
reads as a single blob at 0.78 coverage with a ratio of **90**.

??? note "The `4/π` perimeter correction"
    The digital "crack perimeter" over-estimates a smooth boundary by about `4/π`, so `blobShapes`
    applies that correction, and the gallery measures a synthetic 40-cell disc to confirm it lands at
    1.00. The correction is asymptotic, so a 10-cell blob reads slightly **under** 1 (hence 0.80 for the
    spots). That bias points toward "round", which makes a *stripe* verdict conservative.

Two controls. `v = 0` is a stable fixed point of the equations, so an unseeded field stays at exactly
0.0 forever, so the pattern comes from the dynamics and not from the renderer. And with `Du == Dv` the
Turing instability's short-scale advantage is gone and the same seed, the same reaction and the same
6000 steps produce nothing at all: Turing's own argument, restated as an experiment.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/alife_examples/gray-scott.png" wait="20.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}

What to watch, with the step counter in the caption as your clock:

- **Step ~600.** Every square has buckled into a four-lobed cross. This is the Turing instability

- **Step ~1600.** Each patch has filled its own interior with labyrinth and the fronts are advancing into
  empty substrate. The black regions are unconsumed `u`, and they are shrinking.
- **Step ~2900.** The fronts have met. From here the field is *entirely* labyrinth and the dynamics change
  character completely: no more growth, only rearrangement.
- **Step 6000.** Annealed. Watch the last second and almost nothing moves; the little that does is at the
  free ends, which is where a labyrinth still has somewhere to go. That is why the section's numbers are
  stable enough to assert.

Those five events are not spread evenly through the 6000 steps, so the clip is not paced evenly either.

??? aside "The step schedule here is geometric, not linear"
    Reaction–diffusion is a **log-time** process: step 60 to step 600 and step 600 to step 6000 are about
    equally large *visible* changes, so equal steps per displayed frame cannot be equal change per frame.
    A linear schedule spends four fifths of this clip's change in its first two seconds and then shows a
    finished labyrinth for four.

    of the fence below sets it to 40, meaning the last displayed frame advances forty times as many steps
    as the first, on the geometric schedule `done(t) = 6000 · (40^t − 1) / 39`. The mid-point of the
    *schedule* is then step **819** rather than step 3000, and half the clip's change has arrived at 47.8 %
    of its length rather than at 14.5 %.

    What a ramp cannot do is make a *burst* uniform. Gray–Scott's is the fronts filling the domain, roughly
    steps 400 to 1500, which is 18 % of a linear clip and 30 % of this one. A schedule only decides how
    much of the clip that window gets, and `ramp` is the one parameter to change if you disagree with where
    it sits.

    The ramp asks the last frames for about 170 reaction–diffusion steps each, which is more work than the
    first frames. During docs capture that cost can make the build slower, but cannot stretch or truncate
    the movie: the recorder advances `AnimationClock` by exactly `1 / fps` only after the preceding Field
    frame has been painted and stored. This clip therefore reaches `step 6000 of 6000` reproducibly, with a
    beat of settled labyrinth after it, and the burned-in step clock keeps that endpoint checkable.

## 5. Lenia

Lenia is one field `A` in `0..1`, one convolution kernel `K`, one growth mapping `G`, and

```diffstatic {data-lang=text}
A  <-  clamp(A + dt * G(K * A), 0, 1)
```

That is the whole system. Its interest is that with a smooth ring kernel and a smooth bell-shaped
growth mapping it supports localised, self-maintaining, *moving* structures (solitons), which a
lattice automaton quantises away.

There is a very good cross-check available on an *implementation* of it. With a uniform Moore ring
kernel, `dt = 1`, and a **three-valued** step growth mapping (`+1`
on the birth counts, `0` on survive-only counts, `-1` elsewhere), Lenia reduces exactly to an
outer-totalistic `B/S` rule: `G = +1` forces a cell alive from either state, `G = 0` leaves it as it
was, `G = -1` forces it dead. So this file's sparse float convolution and `alife_ca.kt`'s integer
neighbour counting must agree **bit for bit**.
[`leniaFromLifeRule`](reference/alife.md#alife-continuous-kt) builds that limit, and the worst per-cell
difference over 20 generations of a glider is `0.0`. Moving the growth window one neighbour count
diverges completely.

Be precise about what that proves. These are not two independent implementations of Conway's Life:
`leniaFromLifeRule` reads the very same `B3/S23` birth and survive sets that the integer stepper reads,
so a wrong table would produce two wrong steppers in perfect agreement. What the bit-for-bit result
cross-validates is the two **update mechanisms**: a float convolution, an additive `A + dt·G` step, the
quantisation back to a neighbour count, the clamp to `0..1`, the toroidal border and the `Img`↔`IntGrid`
bridges, against integer neighbour counting and a table lookup. The *rule* is pinned separately, and from
outside this codebase, by the named-object checks above: a glider that translates by exactly `(1, 1)` in
four generations, a block that does not move, a blinker of period 2.

The limit needs `birth ⊆ survive`. If a count births a dead cell but does not sustain a live one, no
function of the neighbour count alone can do both, so `leniaFromLifeRule` rejects the rule rather than
producing a different automaton. Conway's `B3/S23` satisfies it.

For the *continuous* regime this page reports a measured phase trichotomy rather than a named creature.
[`leniaRun`](reference/alife.md#alife-continuous-kt) classifies an outcome as `DEATH`, `BOUNDED` or

## 6. Boids

[Reynolds' three rules](https://www.red3d.com/cwr/boids/) — separation, alignment, cohesion — on a
torus. The
domain wraps for a reason beyond tidiness: in a bounded box the walls do half the flocking, because
agents that bounce off the same wall end up parallel, so a polarization measured in a box is not
evidence about the *rules*.

A flock is two things at once, and both are measured here:

- **Aligned.** The order parameter `|Σ v̂| / N` is 0.692 after 900 steps. That needs a scale, so
  [`randomPolarizationBaseline`](reference/alife.md#alife-kt) gives it: `√π / 2√N` is the expected value
  for `N` *independent* headings, which for 400 agents is 0.044. The measured value is 15.6× that. And
  the same initial state with `alignmentWeight = 0`, nothing else changed, reaches 0.073.
- **Spaced.** The 5th-percentile nearest-neighbour distance is 1.37 cells; with `separationWeight = 0`
  it collapses to 0.01. The floor under that distribution is the separation term, and you can see the
  control arm's population has collapsed to points.

0.692 rather than something near 1 is the *correct* answer, not a weak one: the population settles into
several separate flocks with different headings (visible in the figure), and the global order parameter
of `k` independent flocks tops out near `1/√k`.

??? aside "A stalled flock can still score well on alignment"
    The three steering terms are written as *desired-minus-current* velocities, so in a settled flock
    they largely cancel and, under a force cap, the speed drifts downward: without a floor it lands near
    **0.46** against a cap of 1.4, which is a flock that has mostly stopped while still looking aligned.
    `BoidParams.minSpeedFraction` holds that floor, and it changes magnitude only and never heading, so
    it cannot inflate the polarization number.

interesting event is the rare one: two flocks meeting and either merging or passing through. That is why

## 7. Physarum

Jones' slime-mould model. Each agent deposits into a trail field, samples that field three ways ahead,
turns toward the strongest, and moves. The network is not stored anywhere; it is the fixed point of
that stigmergic loop.

The measurement is [`topShare(0.05)`](reference/alife.md#alife-kt): the fraction of all deposit held by
the brightest 5 % of pixels. A flat field gives 0.05 by definition. The sensing population gives
**0.480**; the identical population with sensing switched off (same count, same seed, same deposit,
same decay, random turns) gives **0.185**. And the shapes differ as sharply: median isoperimetric ratio
17.2 against 1.2, filaments against blobs.

??? aside "Mutual exclusion is the whole model, not an optimisation"
    Without Jones' one-agent-per-cell rule there is nothing to stop every agent within sensing range of
    the brightest trail converging on it, and they do: 6000 agents collapse onto a 191-cell streak and
    measure a top-5 % share of **1.000**, which reads as perfect concentration and is total failure.
    `PhysarumParams.exclusive` makes the population *incompressible*, so a trail can only get so strong
    before it has to widen or branch, and branching under a density limit is what a transport network
    is.

### Watching the network find itself

`topShare` climbing from 0.05 to 0.48 is the evidence; the clip is what the number is *about*. 400 steps
in seven seconds, three per displayed frame, both populations stepped together, with the top-5 % share
recomputed and printed every frame.

Three things to watch, and the third is the one worth waiting for:

1. The disc **expands**, in both panels. That is not the network; that is 6000 mutually exclusive agents
   needing room.
2. In the sensing panel the expansion goes **anisotropic** almost immediately: some directions get
   reinforced and the rest go dark. Nothing chose those directions. They are wherever the deposit happened
   to be a little stronger when the agents first looked.
3. Then the interior **reorganises**: trails that were separate merge, and loops close and re-open. The
   share number keeps climbing while the *shape* keeps changing, because the network is a fixed point of
   the loop rather than something that gets built and then stops.

The blind panel is the same 6000 agents with `sensing = false`, so it expands and then just sits there,
uniform, at a share that stays near a fifth of the sensing run's.

## 8. Diffusion-limited aggregation

Diffusion-limited aggregation: a seed at the centre, then particles released far away that random-walk
until they touch the cluster and stick. Nothing in the rule mentions branches, and the result is a
dendrite.

It is the one system in the family with a quantitative number to hit: the **mass–radius dimension**,
fitted as `N(r) ∝ r^D` in log–log space by
[`massRadiusDimension`](reference/alife.md#alife-kt), which also reports `r²`, because a slope through a
curve is not a dimension. Planar DLA's asymptotic value is about 1.71; the cluster below measures
**1.597** with `r² = 0.9965`.

The two controls are what make that number mean something. An **Eden cluster** uses the same
neighbourhood and the same particle count, and differs only in that the growth site is chosen
uniformly instead of by a diffusing walker: it measures **1.860** and is visibly compact. A **uniform
sprinkle** over the same disc has dimension exactly 2 by construction and measures **1.898**. So the
estimator is reading the diffusion-limited part of DLA and not merely "a growth process happened", and
it is not simply reading the bounded support.

??? aside "Stated as a range, not as a match"
    1.597 is below 1.71 because lattice DLA clusters of this size are known to read low, and the
    asymptote needs far larger clusters. The assertion in CI is therefore "clearly between 1.5 and 1.8,
    and clearly not 2".

    "The cluster reads low" and "the estimator reads low" are different claims, and the second one is
    checkable. A point set placed at radii `R·(i/n)^(1/D)` has
    `N(r) = n·(r/R)^D` **by construction** for any real `D`, and `massRadiusDimension` recovers
    `1.000, 1.262, 1.711, 2.002` from sets built with `D = 1.00, 1.2619, 1.71, 2.00`. Handed something
    whose exponent *is* 1.71 it returns 1.71. Separately, a straight line of lattice points reads 0.993
    and a filled lattice disc 1.986, the same 0.7 % low, because a staircase `N(r)` is not a power law.
    So about 0.7 % of the gap is the lattice and the rest is the cluster's finite size.

    A related trap, also caught by a control: fitting from where `N(r)` is three points measured a
    *uniform disc* at dimension **2.32**, which is not a possible answer. `massRadiusDimension`'s
    `minCount` raises the inner radius until the statistics exist.

### The order the branches arrived in

A DLA cluster's shape is a record of *when*. The cluster is grown **once**, by `dlaCluster`, and
`Aggregate.points` is the order the particles stuck in. The clip reveals that recorded order at a
uniform rate. It is not a re-simulation and it is not uniform in the original walk's wall-clock either: a late particle takes far
longer to arrive than an early one, because it has to random-walk in from a larger circle past a bigger
target. What is uniform is particle *count*.

**Screening.** The interior stops growing almost immediately: once a branch has neighbours on both sides,
a walker arriving from outside is overwhelmingly likely to touch a tip first, so it never reaches the
inside. What grows is a small number of tips racing outward while everything behind them is frozen, and
that is why a mass–radius fit gives 1.6 and not 2: the interior is permanently *empty*, made empty by the
arrival process rather than by the rule.

??? aside "Cropped, and *not* zoomed"
    The same arithmetic as section 1's small boards. A cluster that only ever grows can never differ from
    its first frame by more than the ink it lays down, and on a 300 × 300 domain this cluster lays down
    **2.7 %** of the pixels. Cropping once to the cluster's own bounding box raises that to **6.0 %**, and
    the box below prints both figures from the cluster it is about to animate.

    The crop has to be taken **per axis**. A DLA cluster is *anisotropic*, one arm gets ahead and sets the
    radius, and this one's bounding box is **261 × 152** while a square of side `2 · maxRadius` would be
    282 × 282 and leave the ink share at 3.0 %. `maxRadius` is the right number for fitting a dimension and
    the wrong one for framing a picture.

    A perfect crop is still a couple of percent of ink on black, so this will always be a quieter clip than
    a field that re-colours every cell. The alternative, letting arrival order drive a *growing* crop so
    the view zooms out as the cluster spreads, would destroy the figure: screening is a claim about the
    interior standing still while the tips advance, and in a frame that rescales every step nothing stands
    still. It is exactly the trap [`rasterizeFLinesFramed`](reference/alife.md#alife-animate-kt) avoids in
    section 9, and section 4's fixed colour range avoids in colour.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/alife_examples/dla.mp4" capture="box" open-outputs="true" wait-output="true" wait-output-kind="display" execution="launch" duration="8" fps="20" timeout="240" w="800" embed=true name="alife-dla-video" alt="a diffusion-limited aggregation cluster appearing in the order its particles arrived: a few tips race outward while the interior freezes"}
:::static
// Grow the cluster once, then replay `Aggregate.points` -- which IS the order the particles stuck
// in -- at a uniform rate over seven seconds.
val dla = dlaCluster(300, 300, particles = 6000, seed = 2L)

:::fold crop once to the finished cluster's bounding box, and colour by arrival order on its full scale
// The crop is the colour-range discipline in geometry: taken ONCE, from the finished cluster, never
// from the frame -- a crop that tracked the growing prefix would zoom out as the cluster grew and
// the screening this clip is about would be the one thing you could not see.
//
// Per AXIS rather than a square around maxRadius: a DLA cluster is anisotropic, and maxRadius is set
// by its single longest arm, so a square crop leaves a third of the panel permanently empty.
val pad = 2
val x0 = (dla.points.minOf { it.x }.toInt() - pad).coerceAtLeast(0)
val y0 = (dla.points.minOf { it.y }.toInt() - pad).coerceAtLeast(0)
val cw = (dla.points.maxOf { it.x }.toInt() + pad + 1 - x0).coerceAtMost(300 - x0)
val ch = (dla.points.maxOf { it.y }.toInt() + pad + 1 - y0).coerceAtMost(300 - y0)

// `arrivalPrefixImg` fixes the colour ramp to the FULL cluster's particle count, so a branch keeps
// the colour it arrived with; `arrivalOrderImg` normalises by its own count and would re-map the
// newest particle to the top of turbo on every frame.
fun cluster(dla: Aggregate, n: Int) =
    ["particles " + n + " of " + dla.points.size to
        dla.arrivalPrefixImg(n).crop(x0, y0, cw, ch).colormap("turbo", 0f, 1f).upscaleNearest(3)]
:::endfold

// Why the crop: a cluster is a fixed amount of ink, and how legible its growth is depends entirely on
// how much of the frame that ink occupies. Note the particle count in the first line -- `particles`
// is a ceiling, not a promise, and this cluster stopped well short of the 6000 asked for.
println(dla)
println("cropped to " + cw + " x " + ch + " of 300 x 300, so " +
    "%.1f".format(100.0 * dla.points.size / (cw * ch)) + "% of the panel is ever lit, against " +
    "%.1f".format(100.0 * dla.points.size / 90000.0) + "% uncropped")

animateEvolution(
    Unit,
    totalSteps = dla.points.size,
    seconds = 7.0,
    cellSide = 660,
    step = { it },
    panels = { _, n -> cluster(dla, n) }
)

## 9. L-systems

L-systems are the odd one out in this family. They are the one generative system here whose output can
be checked **exactly and combinatorially**.

- Lindenmayer's original algae system (`A → AB`, `B → A`) has derivation lengths that are the Fibonacci
  numbers. Exactly.
- The Koch snowflake has exactly `3 · 4^n` forward symbols at generation `n`.
- Its turtle path **closes**: the pen returns to where it started, to `2.3 × 10⁻¹⁴` of a step.
- Its drawn length grows by exactly **4×** per generation at constant step size. (The textbook `4/3` is
  the ratio when the figure is held at constant *diameter*; this turtle holds the step constant, so the
  figure triples in size each generation. Same identity, stated for what is actually drawn.)
- And its enclosed area matches the closed form `9^n · A₀ · (1 + 3/5(1 − (4/9)^n))` to `3 × 10⁻⁸`
  relative, a second independent geometric identity from the same turtle. (`FLine` stores
  single-precision coordinates; that residual is the float, not the identity.)

Perturbing the turn angle by 0.01 radians leaves the path open by 2.7 steps, so the closure test has
teeth.

The bracket pair `[` `]` is what makes an L-system a *plant* rather than a curve: it pushes and pops the
turtle state, so a production can grow a side branch and return. And stochastic productions (several
competing rules for one symbol) vary the **topology** rather than jittering one plant's coordinates,
which is why the three plants below have 91, 74 and 51 branches rather than three wobbly copies of the
same tree.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/alife_examples/lsystem.png" wait="6.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}

println("Koch snowflake forward symbols (3 * 4^n): " +

// And the turtle: the path CLOSES, its drawn length quadruples exactly at constant step size, and

### The turtle, walking

An L-system could be animated by *derivation depth*, generation 0 then 1 then 2, and that would be a
slideshow: six generations over seven seconds is 23 duplicate frames between each change, and each
generation is a completely different picture, so there is no motion to read, only cuts.

What an L-system does have is a turtle, and a turtle walks in an order.
[`flinePrefix`](reference/alife.md#alife-animate-kt) truncates the emitted [`FLine`](fline_examples.md)s at a
fraction of their total segment count in walk order, so both panels below are drawn by a pen, in the
sequence the pen moved.

Which makes the bracket pair visible in the right-hand panel. `[` pushes the turtle's state and `]` pops
it, so a plant is drawn **depth-first**: the pen runs all the way out to the tip of one branch, then jumps
back to a fork it remembered and runs out to the next. You can watch it do exactly that, and the jumps are
the stack. The Koch snowflake on the left has no brackets at all and is therefore one
continuous stroke: 768 segments at generation 4, traced without the pen ever leaving the paper, closing
back on its start to `2.3 × 10⁻¹⁴` of a step.

!!! note "The framing has to be pinned, or nothing moves"
    [`rasterizeFLines`](reference/alife.md#alife-lsystem-kt) fits its raster to the bounds of what it is
    given, which for a *growing* curve means the figure is rescaled on every frame: the curve appears to
    stay the same size while the world shrinks around it, and the growth becomes invisible.
    [`rasterizeFLinesFramed`](reference/alife.md#alife-animate-kt) takes the framing from the finished curve
    instead. This is the same class of mistake as an auto-ranged colour map, in geometry rather than in
    colour.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/alife_examples/lsystem.mp4" capture="box" open-outputs="true" wait-output="true" wait-output-kind="display" execution="launch" duration="8" fps="20" timeout="240" w="900" embed=true name="alife-lsystem-video" alt="a Koch snowflake being traced as one continuous stroke beside a bracketed L-system plant drawn depth-first, the pen jumping back to remembered forks"}

// the raster to whatever it is handed, so a growing prefix rescales every frame: the curve appears
// to stay the same size while the world shrinks around it, and the growth becomes invisible.

    val pct = (f * 100).toInt()

        "Koch gen 4: " + pct + "% drawn" to rasterizeFLinesFramed(flinePrefix(koch, f), koch, 420, 420),

    ]
}
:::endfold

// exactly that order. 240 ticks over 140 displayed frames.
val koch = drawLSystem(LSYSTEM_KOCH_SNOWFLAKE, 4, TurtleParams(angle = Math.PI / 3.0, step = 1.0))
val plant = drawLSystem(LSYSTEM_STOCHASTIC_PLANT, 5, TurtleParams(angle = Math.toRadians(24.0), step = 4.0), seed = 1L)
val ticks = 240
animateEvolution(
    Unit,
    totalSteps = ticks,
    seconds = 7.0,
    columns = 2,
    cellSide = 420,
    step = { it },
    panels = { _, n -> drawn(koch.lines, plant.lines, n.toDouble() / ticks) }

    The Sierpiński arrowhead curve is written `A → B−A−B`, `B → A+B+A`, where `A` and `B` are *both*
    drawing symbols. Interpreted with the default `F`/`G` alphabet it draws nothing at all, and a blank
    panel is the only warning you get.

## 10. Bridges out: FLines, trees and a watertight mesh

What makes this family Field's rather than a generic ALife library is where its output goes. Three
bridges, all into machinery that was already here:

1. **A reaction–diffusion field → [`FLine`](fline_examples.md)s.** `Img.isoContourFLines` runs the
   marching-squares extractor in `contours.kt` over the `v` field, so a Gray–Scott result becomes
   drawable, animatable, exportable geometry: 195 contours at `v = 0.25` below. That count is checked
   against a second measurement rather than printed: CI asserts at least one loop per thresholded blob,
   and pins the extractor itself against circle geometry (a disc's contour encloses `πr²` to 0.16 %).
2. **Space colonization → a tree of `FLine`s.** Grown into an *annulus*, which no
   upward-with-noise heuristic reaches, so the branching really is following the space.
   `ColonizationTree.isTree()` checks the thing a picture cannot show (one root, `n − 1` edges, no
   cycles) because a growth algorithm that produces a cycle looks identical.
3. **A 3-D life-like automaton → a [`TriMesh`](mesh_examples.md).** `IntVolume.toMesh` smooths the
   occupancy and runs `mesh_sdf.kt`'s marching cubes, so the automaton's surface is a real mesh you can
   boolean, subdivide and export. The claim asserted is that it is **watertight**: a leaking mesher
   produces a picture that looks fine and a model that cannot be printed.

!!! warning "Contour loops carry no winding information"
    An annulus contours to two loops, an outer and an inner, and **both come back wound the same way**.
    Each is right to better than 0.4 % of its own circle, so the geometry is sound, but
    `loops.sumOf { flineSignedArea(...) }` reads 67 % high for a shape with a hole; the right answer is
    the *difference* of the magnitudes (0.006 % out). Anything that fills, booleans or exports these
    curves has to find the hole by containment or by area, not by orientation.

??? aside "An empty mesh is vacuously watertight"
    A dead volume meshes to **zero triangles** and passes a watertight check, so the triangle count is
    part of the claim.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/alife_examples/bridges.png" wait="16.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20"}

//     `contours.kt` that was already here.

val contours = rd.v.isoContourFLines(0.25, cells = 96)
println("Gray-Scott -> " + contours.size + " iso-contour FLine(s) at v = 0.25")

val tree = spaceColonization(ring, 150.0, 285.0, influenceRadius = 30.0, killRadius = 7.0, stepSize = 5.0)
println(tree)
println("is a tree (one root, n-1 edges, acyclic): " + tree.isTree())
println("CONTROL, no attractors: " + spaceColonization(emptyList(), 150.0, 285.0).nodeCount + " nodes")

println("marched: " + mesh.triangleCount + " triangles, watertight = " + mesh.isWatertight() +

### The bridge, live: a field and its contours at the same time

The first of those three bridges is the one worth animating, because it is the one that produces *geometry*
rather than a picture, and geometry that tracks a moving field is the thing you would actually want in a

The loop count climbs while the spots are dividing, because each division is one loop becoming
two, and it is the one number on this page that is a *topological* measurement rather than a statistical
